section.title: Rationale and purpose of this document
section.para: LinkML schemas are increasingly used to formally describe data models throughout the life sciences (and beyond). This fast adoption creates a need for some guidance to be provided to authors of LinkML schemas, for the following reasons:

listitem.para: There is very little available guidance on how to create schemas that are extensible and reusable.

LinkML’s own documentation is often lacking. Several features are poorly documented, if at all. Among other effects, this can lead some schema authors to devise sometimes needlessly complicated solutions to achieve something that could be done much more easily using available LinkML features, simply because they are unaware of said features or don’t realise what they can be used for.

Several aspects of LinkML are critically underspecified. This means that some features cannot be relied upon, because there are little to no guarantees that they would be supported in the same way across different implementations of LinkML. Importantly, sometimes “different implementations of LinkML” may mean “different parts of the same implementation, so even if you are only using (or planning to use) LinkML-Py (in principle the de facto reference implementation), some underspecified features may still be supported differently depending on which parts (for example, which generator) of LinkML-Py you are using. Underspecified features are also a risk in the long-term, because they may work one way in a given version of LinkML, and another way in a future version.

section.title: Prerequisites
section.para: This document is not intended as a substitute for LinkML’s own documentation. The reader is assumed to have some basic familiarity with LinkML.

This document also assumes that the author of a LinkML schema (i) is also the designer of the model that the schema is supposed to formally represent, and (ii) as such, is free to design the model as required to follow the proposed guidelines.

note.para: This may not always be the case. For example, one may have to author a schema to represent a pre-existing model that one may not be allowed to change – maybe because the model is already in active use, and any change to the model may break existing code or data. In such a scenario where a schema is “retrofitted” to an existing model, several of the guidelines in this document may be impossible to apply.

section.title: About schema reusability
section.para: One particular aims of those guidelines is to promote reusability of LinkML schemas. As a preliminary step, we need to clarify what reusability actually means, and in particular, to clearly distinguish between “reusing a model” and “reusing a schema”.

note.para: Throughout this document, a clear distinction is always made between a model and a schema. Simply put, a schema is a formal description of a model, using a schema definition language (SDL) such as LinkML, XML Schemas, JSON Schema, etc. Among other things, this distinction notably means that, while a schema always corresponds to (formally describes) a single model, the same model can have several formal descriptions as schemas.

section.para:
To illustrate the difference between “reusing a model” and “reusing a schema”, let us consider the case of a model for the concept of “person”. Such a model could define a person as an entity that has a first name, a surname, a date of birth, and an email address.
This would be a very questionable model, if only because the assumption that any person has a first name and a surname is a rather bold one and does not hold in all corners of the world. But it will do for our purpose here.
A LinkML schema for that model could look like this (schema preamble omitted for brevity):

example.title: The “person” schema
example.programlisting: classes: Person: attributes: first_name: range: string surname: range: string birthdate: range: date email: range: string

section.para: Now let us imagine another model that, among other things, also needs to represent “persons”. For example, suppose you want to describe scientific experiments, and you need to capture the person(s) who performed an experiment.

Reusing the “person“ model for this purpose means that you would write your “experiment” schema so that it formally defines the same concept of person, possibly with some specific new attributes. This could look like this:

example.title: The “experiment” schema reusing the person model
example.programlisting:
classes: Experiment: attributes: experimenter: range: Experimenter multivalued: true # Other attributes defining an experiment...
Experimenter: attributes: first_name: range: string surname: range: string birthdate: range: date email: range: string

section.para: In that schema, the Experimenter class describes the same kind of object as the Person class of the previous schema. A JSON dictionary representing a valid Person would also represent a valid Experimenter. However, you will have noticed that there is no link of any kind between the two schemas: the second schema is reusing the model described by the first schema, but it is not reusing the schema itself.
Reusing the schema itself, on the other hand, means that you would import the first schema, and could look like this:

example.title: The “experiment” schema reusing the person schema
example.programlisting:
imports: - person
classes: Experiment: attributes: experimenter: range: Person multivalued: true # Other attributes defining an experiment...

callout.para: This supposes the first schema is available in a file named person.yaml in the same directory as the directory containing this schema.
This is a reference to the Person class from the imported schema.

section.para: The schemas in and in are in effect describing the same model. A bit of instance data valid against the former is also valid against the latter. The difference is that the latter is avoiding duplicating the code from the schema in .
Reusing a model is reasonably easy – it can be done by basically copying the contents of the schema describing the model to reuse, and pasting it into the schema describing the reusing model.

Reusing a schema is more difficult. Or, more precisely, designing a schema in such a way that it can be easily reused (imported) in another schema is more difficult.
Though of course this is not apparent with our “Person” example, given its simplicity. One big aim of this document is to help schema authors to do precisely that.

section.title: About schema extensibility
section.para: Another aim of this document is to promote the extensibility of LinkML schemas.
We define a schema as being “extensible” if it is possible to create modified versions of the schema in such a way that at least some compatibility is preserved between the versions of the schema.

If we assume an original schema S1 and a modified schema S2, as well as a piece of instance data D1 valid against S1 and a piece of instance data D2 valid against S2, we can define the following compatibility scenarios:

listitem.para: No compatibility: D1 is only valid against S1 and D2 is only valid against S2.

Backward compatibility: D1 is additionally valid against S2. Therefore, S2 can be said to be backward-compatible with S1.
There is unfortunately an inherent ambiguity in the use of the words “backward” and “forward”. Here, we use “backward” because we are considering compatibility from the point of view of the schemas: the newer schema (S2) can accept data “from the back” (data that was intended to be valid against the older schema S1).

Backward and forward compatibility: D2 is additionally valid against S1. Therefore S1 can be said to be forward-compatible with S2. Or, we can say that there is bidirectional interoperability between S1 and S2.

section.para: In general, the “no compatibility” scenario must be considered the default outcome whenever a new schema is derived from a pre-existing one, if no special considerations were given to interoperability. One aim of this document is to promote, minimally, “backward compatibility”, and ideally “bidirectional interoperability”.

Of note, it does not really matter who is creating the modified schema S2. It could be a third party independently creating their own “fork” of the original schema for their own needs, or it could also be the authors of the original schema working on a new version intended to supersede the first version. The interoperability concerns remain the same, and making the original schema easily extensible benefits both cases.

Also, as far as interoperability is concerned, it does not really matter whether S2 is derived from S1 by “reusing the model” or by “reusing the schema”. As per , the former would mean that S2 describes the same model as S1 (modulo the S2-specific changes) but is actually independent from S1; the latter would mean that S2 imports S1 and then adds its changes on top of it. In this document, we favour (as already mentioned in the aforementioned section) the reusability of schemas, but the interoperability concerns between S1 and S2 remain the same regardless of how reusability is achieved.

section.title: Extensibility vs flexibility
section.para: We need to further distinguish between a schema that is extensible and a schema that is flexible. Ultimately, both extensibility and flexibility have the same goal: making it possible to use a schema to do things that the original authors of the schema did not imagine – such as dealing with a type of data that they could not have foreseen, or a use case that they did not consider.

In a nutshell, extensibility aims to achieve that goal by making it possible to extend the schema to fit the new requirements; flexibility, by making it possible to use the existing data structures to fit the new requirememts, without having to change (extend) the schema at all.
One way of making a schema flexible is to have some generic data structure, specially reserved for the representation of arbitrary, unknown data.

For example, the SSSOM specification reserves a other field, intended to store arbitrary key-value pairs to allow SSSOM users to store additional mapping metadata, while staying strictly within the boundaries of the SSSOM schema – a SSSOM file may contain dozens or even hundreds of custom properties in its other fields, it will still remain strictly compliant with the SSSOM schema.

Almost by definition, there are always some limits to what is doable with a flexible schema. For example, the aforementioned other field of the SSSOM schema does not allow to store anything else than plain strings (no support for typing or complex structures). Some schemas may have more elaborate generic data structures, possibly with some built-in type system, but this may come at the expense of significant complexity – and may still not be enough to cover all unforeseen use cases.

Another issue with flexibility is that there is typically no way to enforce a consistent and interoperable use of the flexible features. Taking again the SSSOM example, anyone can use the other field to store any additional metadata they want, but there is no guarantee that everyone will understand and know how to exploit said additional metadata. That field can thus easily be abused and lead to SSSOM files that are all compliant with the SSSOM spec, but that cannot be fully understood by anyone else than their original authors.

This document is more concerned about extensibility than flexibility – in fact, one aim of this document is to promote schemas that are easy enough to extend that they don’t need to be very flexible –, but the two concepts are not mutually exclusive. It may be desirable for a schema to be simultaneously (a) flexible enough that at least some basic unforeseen use cases can be covered with just the original schema, and (b) easily extensible so that more complex unforeseen use cases can be dealt with by creating an extended schema.

section.title: Versioning of schemas
section.para:
Any schema that is intended to be reusable outside of the context in which it was originally developed should have a clear versioning policy, describing what downstream users of the schema might expect in the future when newer versions of the schema are released.
We could argue that having a clear versioning policy is useful even for a schema that is not intended to be reused outside of its original context.

section.title: Example: The SSSOM case
section.para:
This document does not want to be too “prescriptive” about the versioning policy, as this is something that may need to be tailored for every individual project. Instead, we will use the versioning policy of the SSSOM specification as an illustrative example.
The fact that the author of this document also happens to be the author of SSSOM’s versioning policy is not a coincidence.

The SSSOM schema uses a fairly common versioning scheme where each version of the schema is identified by two numbers X.Y, where X is the major version and Y is the minor version. The crux of the versioning policy is that the only changes that are allowed in a minor version are changes that do not break backward compatibility with any previous minor version in the same major branch. That is, data that is valid against a version X.Y of the schema must still be considered valid against any version X.Y+n.

Essentially, this means that a minor version can only ever add things to the schema (new classes, new attributes, new enumerations, new permissible values), it can never remove anything. Any removal of an element (e.g. an attribute in a class) could make existing data invalid and is therefore forbidden in a minor version. This prohibition applies to renaming, since renaming an element is in fact no different from (i) adding an element with the new name (which is fine in a minor version), and (ii) removing the element with the old name (which is forbidden).

This also means that a minor version cannot add new constraints, if those constraints are stricter than those of previous minor versions. For example, an integer-typed attribute whose range was previously constrained to a value between 0 and 100 cannot be further constrained to a value between 0 and 50, because this would invalidate existing data where that attribute has a value between 50 and 100 (a contrario, it is fine to relax constraints: a new minor version could perfectly define the new expected range between -100 and 100, because this would not invalidate existing data). Likewise, an attribute that was previously optional cannot be made required.

This does not preclude a minor version from deprecating an element when this is deemed useful – as long as the deprecated element remains in the schema and data that makes use of it is still accepted by the new schema.

Conversely, there are no constraints about what can happen in a new major version. Basically, a new major version of the SSSOM schema, if there is ever one,
There is no plan to ever make a SSSOM 2.0 in the foreseeable future. will have to be considered as a completely new schema, unrelated to any previous major version. As such, there would be absolutely no expectation for the new major version to be backward compatible with previous versions. Depending on the reasons that may justify the new major version, the two following scenarios are equally likely and both valid under the versioning policy:

listitem.para: the authors strive to minimize the breaking changes, changing only the few things that need changing while keeping most of the schema backward compatible whenever possible;

the authors decide that, since the new version will break at least a few things anyway, they will use that opportunity to make a “clean break”, and re-design the schema almost entirely without preserving anything from the previous version.

section.para: When a new major version introduces breaking changes (which is, under the SSSOM versioning policy, kind of the definition of a major version), the authors may want to provide migration paths from the previous major version. With LinkML schemas, presumably the best way to do that would be through LinkML-Map transformations, but this is out of scope for this document.

section.title: Versioning forms
section.para: LinkML schemas can contain, alongside other schema-level metadata (such as who authored the schema and when), an explicit version string in the version metaslot. However, it is important to note that this metaslot is informational only. It has no particular significance and LinkML tools make no use of it.

In fact, more generally LinkML has no built-in support for schema versioning. There is no way, for example, to instruct LinkML to import a particular version of a schema. Controlling which version of a schema is imported must be done outside of the importing schema.

note.para: This may seem like a limitation of LinkML, but it is in fact a fairly common compromise in many programming languages – the issue of dealing with versions is kept out of the language and delegated elsewhere. Look at Python for example: The Python language itself also has no builtin support for versioning. When you write import foo in Python code, at this level you do not control which version of foo will be imported – it will be whichever version happens to be available in the Python environment. Managing versions is done “outside” of the Python code, at the level of the project, using tools such as Poetry or UV.

section.para: This leads us to distinguish between several forms of “schema version”:

listitem.para: the version that may appear in the URI of all the elements defined by the schema – we will call that the “element URI version”.

section.para: As already noted, the schema version proper is informational only; the publication version is the one that can actually be used to control which particular version of a schema is used (in particular, which version is imported, when the schema is reused by another importing schema); and the element URI version is the one that matters when working in RDF context.

Of note, the publication version and the URI version may not exist – there is no requirement for any version information to appear in the URI at which a schema is published and in the URIs identifying schema elements. But we recommend that such version information should in fact be present in those URIs.

Consequently, we also recommend that schema authors think carefully about they are going to manage the three different versions. As for the versioning policy itself, this may need to be tailored for the needs of every project, but we make the following suggestions:

listitem.para: The schema version proper should always be set to the “full” version of the schema – that is, it should contain all the components that make up the version, if the versioning policy calls for a version made of several components (e.g. the major and minor version numbers, as in the SSSOM example).

The publication URI should similarly mention all components. However, if the versioning policy specifies that some versions are expected to be backward compatible, then there may also be an additional, single publication URI for all versions where backward compatibility is preserved. That URI can then be made to point to the most recent backward compatible version. For example, assuming a versioning policy similar to the one used by SSSOM, there could be a single URI mentioning only the major version number X, that could be made to point initially to version X.0 of the schema, then to version X.1 when it is available, then to version X.2, and so forth.

The element URI version should preferably omit any version component that does not convey a backward-incompatible change. Taking again the example of SSSOM’s versioning policy, that means that the URIs identifying schema elements (typically automatically derived from the schema’s default_prefix setting) should only contain the major version number.

section.title: Embedding fine-grained version information in the schema
section.para: If the versioning policy specifies that some versions should be backward-compatible, then it is possible to encode directly in the latest version in the schema the differences between that version and any previous version it is backward-compatible with.

We will again take the SSSOM schema as an example, where a new minor version should remain backward-compatible with any previous minor version in the same major branch – meaning, as we have already seen, that the new minor version can only add new elements to the schema.
In the SSSOM schema, any element added in a minor version is explicitly tagged with a custom structured annotation indicating in which version of the schema the element was added:

example.title: Addition of a new element in the SSSOM schema
example.programlisting:
enums: sssom_version_enum: permissible_values: "1.0": title: SSSOM specification version 1.0 "1.1": title: SSSOM specification version 1.1
classes: Versionable: attributes: added_in: range: sssom_version_enum
slots: predicate_type: instantiates: - sssom:Versionable annotations: added_in: "1.1"

callout.para: This is an enumeration that lists the available versions of the SSSOM schema. This is used to constrain the value of the custom annotation added_in.

This is what LinkML calls a “meta-model extension”. It defines the structure of the custom annotations we want to add to some schema elements. Here, the extension defines a single annotation called added_in, whose value should be one of the permissible values of the sssom_version_enum enumeration.

This is an example of a slot that was added in version 1.1 of the SSSOM schema.
The SSSOM schema, while it is being used as an example here, does not follow all the recommendations from this document (which did not exist when the schema was first designed). For example, it abundantly uses slots rather than attributes, contrary to the recommendation in .

This indicates that the element being defined (the predicate_type slot) is making use of the Versionable meta-model extension – that is, it is annotated using the attributes defined in that extension. Note that, contrary to almost all other situations in LinkML where a class is referenced, a meta-model extension is referenced by its URI, not by its name, hence the sssom:Versionable.
This is the actual annotation that indicates that this slot is an addition from version 1.1 of the schema.

section.para: The added_in annotations are completely ignored by LinkML tools, for which they have no particular meaning. But they can be used by any custom tool that is aware of them. For example, both the Java and the Python implementations of the SSSOM specification are using them to automatically determine the lowest version of the specification a SSSOM mapping set is compliant with (by checking in which versions all the slots using by the mapping set were added), or to force a set to be compliant with a given version (by removing all slots that were added in a later version).

It would also be fairly easy to use those annotations to remove from the schema all the elements that were added from version, say, 1.2 onwards, and therefore to obtain a schema that is in effect identical to version 1.1 of the schema (containing all the elements from version 1.0 and the additions from version 1.1, but nothing from the more recent versions).
LinkML subsets could also potentially be used for a similar purpose. But the author of this document believes structured annotations are more flexible.

note.para: This example illustrates the usefulness of LinkML’s annotation system in general, beyond the use case for versioning. As a general rule, we recommend using custom structured annotations whenever you wish to express a specificity of your schema for which LinkML has no builtin metaslot (rather than, say, merely describe the specificity in plain text in the description of an element). Even if LinkML tools will not use them, they can still be exploited by a small custom layer on top of LinkML.

Such custom annotations can also potentially act as a “testbed” for testing putative future metaslots “in the wild” before proposing them for addition to LinkML, if they are deemed to be of a general interest and not too specific to a particular schema.

section.title: What’s in a name?
section.para: All elements within a LinkML schemas (in particular, all definitions, i.e. class definitions, slot definitions, enum definition, etc.) have a name. The name of an element has several purposes, but its primary purpose is to allow referencing the element from elsewhere in the schema – that is, it acts as the identifier for the element.

note.para: Schema elements also have a URI, which is either explicitly assigned by the schema author (using metaslots such as class_uri or slot_uri) or automatically derived from the schema’s default prefix and the element’s name.

However, while the URI of an element may identify the element in some contexts (typically in RDF context), as a general rule it is not an identifier. Elements in a LinkML schemas are strictly identified by their name, not by their URI.

section.para: The name of an element may also fulfil at least two other purposes:

listitem.para: It may directly dictate how the element is supposed to appear in instance data in some serialisations. This is the case, in particular, for slots/attributes and for permissible values.
It serves as the basis from which the code symbol representing the element in a programming language is derived, when generating code for that programming language from the schema.

section.title: Lack of namespacing
section.para: An important aspect of LinkML, which is in fact critical when talking about schema reusability, is that all element names reside in a single, flat namespace.

That namespace encompasses the entire imports closure, which means that when a schema Foo imports another schema Bar, all the elements defined within Bar become available in Foo under their original name. Simply put, this means that if the two schemas happen to each define an element with the same name, a name conflict will occur.

note.para: What happens exactly in this situation – how the name conflict is handled – is currently unclear, as different parts of the reference implementation of LinkML have different behaviours. The most commonly observed behaviour – and presumably the one that is intended to become standardized – is that the element defined in the importing schema will take precedence over the element defined in the imported schema (that is, the element from the imported schema will be completely “masked” by the element from the importing schema).

section.para: As a consequence, schema authors should think very carefully about how they name the elements of their schema, if they intend for the schema to be reusable. In particular, they should refrain, as much as possible, from “cluttering” the global namespace with element names that are too “generic”, because such names increase the likelihood of a naming conflict when the schema is reused (imported) elsewhere.

section.title: LinkML names in data
section.para: Some LinkML names within a LinkML schema have a direct influence on the way the data is serialised, and this must be taken into account when deciding how to name a given schema element.
To understand this, let us consider the following schema:

example.title: A schema for “organisations”
example.programlisting:
classes: Organisation: description: An organisation of some sort. tree_root: true attributes: name: description: The name of the organisation range: string foundation: description: The date the organisation was founded. range: date founder: description: The person who founded the organisation. range: Person type: description: The type of organisation. range: OrganisationType
Person: description: A human person. attributes: first_name: The person’s first name. description range: string surname: description: The person’s surname (or last name, or family name). range: string email: description: The person’s email address. range: string
enums: OrganisationType: description: Possible types for an organisation. permissible_values: commercial: description: An organisation that is a commercial entity. non_profit: description: A non-profit organisation.

section.para: Now let us look at a possible piece of instance data that matches this schema:

example.title: A JSON file representing an organisation

section.para: The important thing to notice in that example is that class names do not appear in the instance data. The fact that the top-level object is an Organisation is not explicitly apparent, and neither is the fact that the value of the founder key is a Person. If those classes had been given other names in the LinkML schema (maybe OrganisationalEntity and PersonalEntity, for example), this would not have changed anything to the way the data is serialised. The file in would still have represented valid data.

Likewise for enumeration names. The fact that the value of the type key is a OrganisationType is not apparent. The enumeration could have been named differently, without impacting the serialisation and therefore without invalidating our example file.

Attribute (or slot) names, on the other hand, do appear in the instance data. The dictionary key names are taken verbatim from the attribute names in the LinkML schema. Should any of the attribute have been named differently, our data file would no longer be valid against the schema.

Likewise for the names of enumerations’ permissible values: the value in the type key must match the name of one of the permissible values of the OrganisationType enumeration. Should those values have been named, say, CommercialEntity and NonProfitEntity, again, our data file would be invalid.

What this all means is that: (i) not all LinkML names are equals, and (ii) for some elements, the choice of the name matters beyond the LinkML schema. As a general rule, when naming classes and enumerations, schema authors have more freedom than when they are naming attributes/slots and permissible values, because the former have no bearing on the serialised data.
There is one case where the name of a class can appear in serialised data: when type designators are used. That case will be covered elsewhere in this document.

note.para: In particular, in the case where a schema is authored a posteriori to fit pre-existing JSON data, the authors of such a retrofitted schema have no freedom at all when it comes to naming the attributes/slots or permissible values: they must use the names as they appear in the existing data.

For example, the Protégé ontology editor has a concept of “deprecation profile” to control what the editor should do when obsoleting a term. A deprecation profile is a YAML file that can look like this:
note.programlisting: --- name: Gene Ontology (GO) description: A profile for obsoletion of entities in the Gene Ontology (GO) activatedBy: http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/go.owl removeLogicalDefinition: true removeAnnotationAssertions: false replacedByAnnotationPropertyIri: IAO:0100001 labelPrefix: obsolete annotationValuePrefix: OBSOLETE. preservedAnnotationAssertionPropertyIris: - IAO:0000115 textualReasonAnnotationPropertyIri: rdfs:comment
note.para: There is currently no formal schema (in LinkML or any other schema definition language) for a deprecation profile, but it would be easy to make one in LinkML.

However, while the authors of such a schema would be free to name the root class however they like (maybe DeprecationProfile or ProtegeDeclarationProfile), they would have no choice when it comes to naming the attributes. They could not, for example, rename the removeLogicalDefinition key into remove_logical_definition, even if that’s what the LinkML linter tool would recommend to follow the LinkML convention of using “snake case” for attribute and slot names.

section.title: Recommended naming conventions
section.para: We recommend the following conventions for naming elements within a LinkML schema. Several of them are already recommended by the LinkML project itself (for those, the linkml lint tool can be used to, among other things, check whether your schema is properly following them).

section.title: Classes
section.para: Use “Pascal case” (no spaces between capitalized words, LikeThis; also known as “upper camel case”). Make sure to use names that are distinctive enough to reduce the likelihood of name conflict if the schema is reused (imported) by another schema; the easiest way to achieve that is to choose a suitable “prefix” and to prepend it to all names.

note.para: We do not mean a CURIE-like prefix, where the prefix is separated from the base name by a colon (as in Prefix:Name)! Instead, we mean a prefix that becomes integral part of the name. That prefix should be, as much as possible, specific to the schema.

For example, the proposed schema for the version 1.1 of the Persistent Identification of Instruments specification will use a PIDInst prefix, yielding class names such as PIDInstOwner, PIDInstManufacturer, etc.

section.para: If the presence of the prefix is not desired in the RDF representation of the data (where it would indeed not be needed, since RDF properties are identified by full URIs rather than mere names and are therefore much less likely to conflict across schemas), it is always possible to explicitly specify the class URI for each class (instead of letting LinkML infer it from the schema’s default prefix and the class’ name) so that it does not include the prefix:

example.title: Explicitly specifing a prefix-less class URI
example.programlisting:
prefixes: myschema: https://example.org/myschema/ default_prefix: myschema
classes: MySchemaManufacturer: class_uri: myschema:Manufacturer

callout.para: All classes in this schema are by convention prefixed with MySchema. This reduces the likelihood of name conflicts when the schema is reused in another context, since Manufacturer is a pretty generic name.

The class URI is explicitly set to https://example.org/myschema/Manufacturer. By default, the inferred class URI would have been https://example.org/myschema/MySchemaManufacturer, which would have been needlessly redundant – in RDF context, the https://example.org/myschema/ URI prefix already confers unicity.

section.title: Mixin classes
section.para: Mixin classes are merely a special type of class. They should use the same convention as for other classes, but with an explicit Mixin suffix appended to the name.
For example, a mixin class that would originally be named Foo should in fact be named MySchemaFooMixin (where MySchema is the schema-specific prefix prepended to all class names, as per ).

The Mixin suffix makes it easier to instantly figure out whether a given class is a mixin class or a “normal” (i.e., non-mixin) class. This in turn makes it easier to spot possible misuses of mixin classes, such as making a non-mixin class inherit (through is_a) from a mixin class – something that is formally forbidden in LinkML, but that most LinkML tools do not adequately flag as a schema error.

section.title: Classes that are only used in one context
section.para: Sometimes, a schema may need a class to describe a complex (non-scalar) type of value that will only ever be used for one particular attribute of one particular class.
For example, let us suppose you need a Person class in which you can also store information about the computer account of the person, as in:

The value expected under the account_info attribute is a complex one, that can only be described by a class in LinkML. And even if that class is never used for anything else than to specify the range of the account_info attribute, that is irrelevant for LinkML, which has no concept such as a “local” or “inline” class definition (defining a class only where it is used). All class definitions in LinkML are necessarily global.

In such a case, it might be useful to name the class in such a way that makes it clear that the class is only intended to ever be used for a particular attribute of a particular “enclosing” class. We do not make any strong recommendation here, but we would suggest something like MySchemaPersonAccountInfo (MySchema being the schema-specific class suffix, Person being the base name of the enclosing class, and AccountInfo being derived from the name of the attribute).

section.title: Slots and attributes
section.para: Use “snake case” (lowercase words separated by underscores, like_this) for the names of slots and attributes, unless pre-existing data forces you to do otherwise.

We do not recommend prefixing slot names with a schema-specific prefix, as we do for class names. This is because, as explained in , slot names directly “leak” into instance data, and a schema-specific prefix would most likely be undesired in most cases.
Instead, to avoid name conflicts between slots across several schemas, we more radically recommend avoiding slots altogether, as explained later in .

section.title: Enumerations and permissible values
section.para: Enumeration names should follow the same conventions as class names (), including the case where an enumeration is only used once throughout the entire schema (). We do not recommend appending a Enum suffix to the name – instead, we suggest that the name of an enumeration should indicate what one of the permissible values is, not what the enumeration itself is (which is also why the name should be in singular form, not in plural form).

Names of permissible values (PVs) should be decided carefully, keeping in mind that, like the names of slots and attributes, they “leak” into instance data (but unlike slot names, PV names do not live in the global namespace – they are local to the enumeration that defines them, so name conflicts between PV names across enumerations – let alone across schemas – are not a thing to worry about).
We do not make strong recommendation regarding the style of PV names (e.g. Pascal case, snake case, etc.). We only strongly recommend to

listitem.para: use a consistent style, whatever it is: for example, avoid mixing Pascal-cased and snake-cased PV names in the same schema (a fortiori in the same enumeration);
avoid spaces, and more generally (though it may not always be possible) any kind of “special” characters.

section.para: When a PV name does contain special characters (and especially if it starts with a special character), we do strongly recommend to assign to it a title free of special characters. This is to allow LinkML code generators to produce developer-friendly symbols for the permissible values.

For example, the schema describing the SSSOM specification defines a MappingCardinality enumeration with permissible values such as 1:1 or 1:n. Without any explicitly specified title, LinkML code generators would produce code symbols like NUMBER1_COLON1 (because they must follow the syntactic rules of the language they are producing code for, and many languages do not allow a code symbol to start with a number – hence the starting “1” being rendered as NUMBER1), which is unwieldy and meaningless. To avoid this, the PVs are given a title from which the code generator can derive more meaningful symbols:

example.title: Permissible values with explicit titles
example.programlisting: enums: MappingCardinality: permissible_values: "1:1": title: one to one "1:n": title: one to many

callout.para: This is the name of the permissible value, as it must appear in instance data.
This will make the code generators produce a symbol like ONE_TO_ONE to represent this PV in code.

section.para: Another case where explicitly assigning titles to permissible values is a good idea is when an enumeration has PVs that differ only by their case:

example.title: Permissible values with case-sensitive names
example.programlisting: enums: ElectricalPotentialUnit: permissible_values: mV: title: milli volt MV: title: mega volt

section.para: Most, if not all, code generators in LinkML would not know how to deal with this situation without the explicitly assigned titles: they would generate the same symbol (MV) to represent both the mV and the MV values (which would most likely trigger a compilation error when the generated code is later used).

section.title: Favour attributes over slots
section.para: LinkML has two different ways of defining what most programming languages would call the fields (sometimes member fields) of a class: slots and attributes.

The two methods are very similar (and not mutually exclusive: a class can have both slots and attributes), the key difference being that slots are defined at the level of the entire schema while attributes are defined within the context of a particular class. Basically, attributes are class-specific slots, or if we prefer the other way round, slots are schema-wide attributes. That difference aside, slots and attributes are equivalent.
At least in theory. In practice, bugs in LinkML-Py may mean that some slot-related feature won’t necessarily always work when they are applied to attributes.
This means the following two schemas are describing the same model:

example.title: A class with slots
example.programlisting:
slots: first_name: description: The first name of a person. range: string last_name: description: The last name of a person. range: string birthdate: description: The date a person was born. range: date
classes: Person: description: Represents an individual person. slots: - first_name - last_name - birth_date

example.title: A class with attributes
example.programlisting: classes: Person: description: Represents an individual person. attributes: first_name: description: The first name of a person. range: string last_name: description: The last name of a person. range: string birthdate: description: The date a person was born. range: date

section.para: The only difference between these two schemas is that, in the first one, the first_name, last_name, and birthdate slots could be reused in another class than just the Person class, whereas in the second schema, the attributes are explicitly specific to the Person – if we wanted to define another class (unrelated to Person) that needed the same attributes, we would need to define the attributes again in that other class.

Slots are sometimes useful, but they cause a major problem for schema reusability: they pollute the global namespace. And because their names directly impact the serialisation of data (as explained in ), you cannot always use naming conventions to help avoiding name clashes.
We will see later () that slot aliases can serve as a workaround for that. Still, it is better to avoid having to use a workaround to begin with.

Another problem (though much more minor) with slots is that, when they are only used in one class, they needlessly separate the various parts that make up the definition of the class, and make the schema more difficult to read. In , this is not apparent because the schema is simplistically small (so the slot definitions can sit just next to the definition of the class in which they are used), but it will become apparent in any medium- or large-sized schema.

Consequently, it is strongly recommended to favour the use of attributes whenever possible. Always start designing your classes with attributes, and only consider turning a local attribute into a global slot when it becomes clear that you will need the very same attribute, with the very same meaning, in more than one class.

section.title: About slot aliases
section.para: A possible workaround for the problem of slot names polluting the global namespace (but one that is still best avoided when possible) is to use slot aliases.

Any slot (or any attribute) in a LinkML schema can have an alias, set forth by the alias metaslot.
Not to be confused with the aliases metaslot – that one is intended to facilitate mappings between a LinkML schema and other resources, but (contrary to alias), it has no significance within the schema. When that is the case, then the defined alias is used for almost all purposes where the slot name would normally be used. The slot name’s remaining purpose is to refer to the slot from within the schema, for example when listing it as one of the slots used by a class.
For an example of how slot aliases can be used, one needs look no further than in LinkML’s own meta-schema, which contains the following:

example.title: LinkML’s “slots” and “slot_definitions” slots (simplified excerpt)
example.programlisting:
slots: slot_definitions: description: All slots defined in this schema. range: slot_definition multivalued: true inlined: true alias: slots
slots: description: All slots applicable to a class. range: slot_definition multivalued: true
classes: schema_definition: description: A single LinkML schema. slots: - slot_definitions
class_definition: description: The definition of a LinkML class. slots: - slots

section.para: The problem that the LinkML developers were facing when authoring their meta-schema is that the name slots is used in two different places within a LinkML schema, with two completely different meanings:

listitem.para: in a “schema definition” (that is, at the root of a LinkML schema file), this is where all the slots are defined;
in a “class definition”, this is where you list the slots that are applicable to that particular class.

section.para: But with slot names being global, it is not possible to have two different slots with the same name, even if they are only used in two completely different contexts! So the workaround was to name the first slot (the one used in a schema definition, where slots are defined) slot_definitions, so that the name would not conflict with that of the other slot (the one used in a class definition). And slot_definitions was given the alias slots, so that it could appear under this name at the root level of a LinkML schema file.

If that sounds needlessly complicated and confusing, it’s because it is. It would have been much more straigthforward and easier, given that both slots are each only used in one class, to define them as attributes of their respective class, as follows:

example.title: LinkML’s “slots” defined as local attributes
example.programlisting:
classes: schema_definition: description: A single LinkML schema. attributes: slots: description: All slots defined in this schema. range: slot_definition multivalued: true inlined: true
class_definition: description: The definition of a LinkML class. attributes: slots: description: All slots applicable to this class. range: slot_definition multivalued: true

section.para: So while slot aliasing can allow to work around the issue caused by slot names being global, the use of local (class-specific) attributes is overall a much simpler solution, and needlessly defining global slots while giving them aliases to avoid name clashes has to be considered a anti-pattern.

section.title: Grouping reusable attributes in mixins
section.para: An alternative to (global) slots, when you have several attributes that should be reused in several unrelated classes, is to declare the attributes in a dedicated mixin class.

For example, let us suppose that many classes in your schema should have the following three attributes: name, identifier, and identifier_type. The classes where those attributes are not related – they don’t share a single parent class in which you could define the attributes once and for all and have them inherited by all the classes. At first sight, this leaves you with two options:

listitem.para: defining the attributes in all the classes that need them – this would lead, by design, to many duplicated definitions, and to a lot of churn whenever an attribute would need to be updated (it would need to be updated in all the classes in which it is defined);

defining the attributes as slots instead – they would need to be defined only once, but then you are polluting the global namespace (which is especially problematic with names as generic as name or identifier).

section.para: Neither solution is particularly satisfying, but luckily, there is a third one: create a single mixin class, define the shared attributes in that class, and then make all the classes that need those attributes inherit from the mixin. This could look like this:

example.title: Using a mixin to group shared attributes
example.programlisting:
classes: IsIdentifiableMixin: description: An entity that can be identified by a name or an identifier. mixin: true attributes: name: description: The name of the entity. range: string identifier: description: An identifier for the entity. range: string identifier_type: description: The type of identifier. range: string
ResearchInstrument: description: Any kind of research hardware (e.g. microscope, centrifuge, etc.). mixins: - IsIdentifiableEntity
InstrumentManufacturer: description: A company (or other organisation) that makes research instruments. mixins: - IsIdentifiableEntity

callout.para: In a real schema this would likely be an enumeration, but for this example a string will do.

section.para: This approach allows to define the attributes only once without polluting the global namespace – the only global name added is that of the mixin, but since this a class name, it does not appear in instance data and we are free to use any naming convention aiming at reducing name clashes with other class names.

note.para: An additional benefit of this approach is that it allows, if needed, to define once and for all in the mixin some rules that should apply to all the classes that inherit the mixin.

For example, suppose you want to enforce that, whenever a identifier value is present, a identifier_type should be present as well. If the attributes had been defined as (global) slots, such a rule would have had to be defined in every class in which the identifier and identifier_type are applicable. But with the attributes defined in the IsIdentifiableMixin, the rule can be defined in that mixin instead – classes that inherit the mixin will get both the attributes and the associated rules!

section.title: Prefer a list of type-designated components over named attributes
section.para: A single multi-valued attribute with a range set to a type-designated class can conveniently replace a series of attributes.

To illustrate, let us suppose you are modelling a computer and its hardware peripheral devices (e.g. keyboard, mouse, webcam, monitor, printer…). Each device, as well as the computer itself, is represented by a distinct class. To model the relations between the computer and the various devices, one possibility would be for the class representing the computer to have one attribute for each different type of peripheral devices, as in the following example:

example.title: Peripherals as separate, specific attributes
example.programlisting:
classes: Computer: attributes: keyboard: range: Keyboard mouse: range: Mouse monitors: range: Monitor multivalued: true printer: range: Printer
Keyboard: Mouse: Monitor: Printer:

callout.para: We omit the detailed definitions for the classes representing the peripheral devices, they are not relevant for this example.

section.para: This would work fine, but is quite cumbersome as every type of peripheral device needs both its own class and its own attribute on the Computer class. This can make the definition of that class quite large (as large as the list of known types of devices). This also means that it is not possible to add a new type of device without changing the Computer class.
We recommend considering an alternative design where the Computer class has instead a single attribute holding a list of devices of any type:

example.title: Peripherals as a list of generic devices
example.programlisting:
classes: Computer: attributes: devices: range: PeripheralDevice multivalued: true
PeripheralDevice: attributes: type: designates_type: true type: string
Keyboard: is_a: PeripheralDevice
Mouse: is_a: PeripheralDevice
Monitor: is_a: PeripheralDevice
Printer: is_a: PeripheralDevice

callout.para: This will store all the devices attached to this computer, regardless of their exact type.
This is the parent class for all types of peripheral devices.
This is the type designator for the PeripheralDevice class. We need it to know the exact type of each device in the devices list.

The type designator could also be a URI and/or a CURIE – and in fact later in this document we will recommend that type designators should be URI/CURIE-typed, but this is out of scope for this example.
All classes representing peripheral devices are subclasses of PeripheralDevice, allowing them to be used in the PeripheralDevice-typed devices list.

section.para: Compared to the previous example, in this design the Computer is kept much simpler, and it will not need to be updated whenever a new type of peripheral will be added to the model – adding a new subclass of PeripheralDevice is all it would take to make the new type usable in the devices list.

note.para: The disdvantage of this design is that it does not allow to express peripheral-specific constraints, such as “there must be at least one keyboard” or “there cannot be more than three monitors”. This does not negate its benefits in terms of simplicity and extensibility, but may require careful consideration.

section.title: Avoid enum inheritance
section.para: In theory, enum inheritance allows to define an enumeration by building on top on another, pre-existing enumeration – very much like class inheritance allows to build a class on top of another class. For example, if you have an enumeration Foo that contains a dozen of permissible values and you need another enumeration Bar which should contain with those same values plus some additional values, it might be convenient to make Bar inherit from Foo, so that you don’t have to define the common dozen of values twice (once in each enumeration).

However, while that possibility theoretically exists in LinkML, it should not be used, at least for the time being. Enum inheritance in LinkML is plagued by two issues that make the feature unreliable.
The first issue is that there are two different ways of making an enum inherit from another:

listitem.para: using the is_a metaslot (the same already used for class and slot inheritance);
using the inherits metaslot.

section.para: It is unclear which of those two slots should actually be used to make an enumeration inherit from another, because LinkML’s meta-schema is contradicting its own documentation here: according to the documentation, the is_a metaslot is only intended for classes and slots, but the schema actually allows the use of is_a on enumerations. And at least parts of the LinkML-Py reference implementations only expect is_a, not inherits to be used on enumerations – even though inherits is the metaslot that the documentation clearly presents as being intended for enumerations.

The second issue is that support for enum inheritance (whether through is_a or through inherits) in LinkML-Py is pretty scarce, almost inexistent. In particular, as far as the author of this document is aware, none of the code generators support it. SchemaView, the main object in LinkML-Py to access the contents of a schema, does provide methods to get the “parent” of an enumeration (through is_a only, not through inherits) but does not allow to infer the “induced permissible values” (values that should be inherited from the parent).

Therefore, and at least until (1) the uncertainty about the intended proper way of making an enum inherit from another is lifted,
LinkML developers are nominally aware of that uncertainty, see LinkML issues #3957 and #3958. and (2) enum inheritance starts getting actual support in the reference implementation – which probably cannot happen until (1) is solved –, enum inheritance is best avoided.

section.title: Anti-patterns
section.para: This section describes typical mistakes that have been observed in some LinkML schemas, and how to avoid them.

section.title: Implementing references
section.para: Let us suppose you need a schema to model books and their authors. You expect to have many books and many authors, with each book being possibly authored by more than one author and each author possibly having authored more than one book. You do not want to have to repeat any information more than necessary – for example, if an author wrote two books, you do not want your data to contain the first name, last name, date of birth, and any other biographical information about the author twice (once for each book).
A naive way to do this would be using the following schema:

example.title: The wrong way of implementing references
example.programlisting:
classes: BookDatabase: description: The object holding the lists of books and authors. tree_root: true attributes: books: description: The list of books in this database. range: Book multivalued: true authors: description: The list of authors in this database. range: Author multivalued: true
Book: description: An individual book. attributes: title: range: string authored_by: description: Identifiers for the author(s) of this book. The value must match the idendifier of an Author object. range: string multivalued: true
Author: description: An individual author. attributes: id: description: Unique identifier for this author. range: string first_name: range: string last_name: range: string birthdate: range: date biography: range: string

section.para: The example is pretty straightforward. In a data definition language such as SQL, the id attribute of the Author class would be called the primary key of the authors table, while the authored_by attribute of the Book class would be called the foreign key of the books table.

The problem with that approach, though, and the reason it is an anti-pattern in LinkML, is that it does not use LinkML’s builtin cross-referencing feature. As a result, there is nothing in the schema itself that can enforce the fact that a value in the authored_by attribute of a book must match the id value of an author. That constraint is only stated in the description of the authored_by attribute, but this is merely a statement of intention that has no real effect whatsoever. Actually enforcing the constraint is entirely left at the discretion of the users of the schema (especially, the developers who will use that schema in their programs).

In LinkML, whenever a class has an attribute or a slot that is explicitly marked as being the identifier for the class (by means of the identifier metaslot), then by default, any attribute or slot (anywhere else in the schema) whose range is set to that class is expected to contain a reference to an object of that class, rather than the object itself.

This means that in our example, all we need to do to use the proper pattern is to (1) mark the id attribute of the Author as being the identifier for the class, and (2) set the range of the authored_by attribute to Author. (We also need to set inlined: true in the definition of the authors attribute in the BookDatabase, because here we do not want to store references only: this is where the authors are defined, so we need the full objects, not mere references.)

example.title: LinkML-powered cross-references
example.programlisting:
classes: BookDatabase: description: The object holding the lists of books and authors. tree_root: true attributes: books: description: The list of books in this database. range: Book multivalued: true authors: description: The list of authors in this database. range: Author multivalued: true inlined: true inlined_as_list: true
Book: description: An individual book. attributes: title: range: string authored_by: description: The author(s) of this book. range: Author multivalued: true
Author: description: An individual author. attributes: id: description: Unique identifier for this author. range: string identifier: true first_name: range: string last_name: range: string birthdate: range: date biography: range: string

callout.para: This marks id as the identifier attribute of the Author class.

Since Author has an identifier attribute, setting the range of authored_by to Author automatically means that this is attribute is expected to contain identifiers of Author objects, rather than the objects themselves.

Now that Author has an identifier attribute, this is required to override the default behaviour that would make this attribute expect references instead of objects – the same behaviour that we want for the authored_by attribute, but that we do not want here.

This forces the list of Author objects to be represented as a real list, rather than as identifier-indexed dictionary. I recommend always setting inlined_as_list explicitly whenever you set inlined: true, because it is unclear, in the LinkML specification, what the default value of inlined_as_list should be.

section.para: That last schema is very similar to the schema in , and importantly, it describes exactly the same model. The difference is that the “foreign key” constraint on the authored_by attribute is no longer a mere statement of intention – it is an actual constraint that can be enforced by LinkML-aware tools.

section.title: Enum-controlled attributes variability
section.para: “Enum-controlled attributes variability” is a terribly bad name, but the (anti-)pattern it attempts to describe is a very common one. This is what happens when you try to use a single class to represent a variety of objects of slightly different types, described by slightly different attributes. And then a single special attribute within the class is used to distinguish between the different types the class is intended to represent.
A simplistic typical example in LinkML could look like this:

example.title: Representing vehicles with a single class with variable attributes
example.programlisting:
enums: VehicleType: description: The type of a vehicle. permissible_values: bicycle: motorbike: car:
classes: Vehicle: attributes: type: description: The type of the vehicle. range: VehicleType mass: description: The mass of the vehicle (when empty), expressed in kg. range: integer power: description: The power of the engine, expressed in horsepower (hp). This attribute should only be filled when type is set to either motorbike or car. range: integer windshield_surface: description: The surface of the windshield, expressed in cm². This attribute should only be filled when type is set to car. range: integer

section.para: A slightly more refined version would use LinkML rules to enforce the constraints that some of the attributes of the Vehicle class can only be used when the type attribute is set to a particular VehicleType value. However, while such rules would allow the schema to work as expected, they could quickly become very cumbersome to maintain.

LinkML provides a much better and easier way of achieving the desired result, which is why has to be considered an anti-pattern. The recommended way in LinkML to implement that example is to use a hierarchy of classes whose base class carries a type designator attribute, as in the following example:

example.title: Representing vehicles with a hierarchy of type-designated classes
example.programlisting:
classes: Vehicle: description: The base class for all types of vehicle. attributes: type: description: The type of vehicle. range: string designates_type: true mass: description: The mass of the vehicle (when empty), expressed in kg. range: integer
Bicycle: is_a: Vehicle
MotorizedVehicle: is_a: Vehicle attributes: power: description: The power of the engine, expressed in horsepower (hp). range: integer
Motorbike: is_a: MotorizedVehicle
Car: is_a: MotorizedVehicle attributes: windshield_surface: description: The surface of the windshield, expressed in cm².

callout.para: This makes type the type designator for the Vehicle class – the attribute whose value indicates the type of the object it belongs to.

This class is not strictly speaking needed, but it allows to avoid repeating the power attribute (or any other attribute that would be shared by all motorized vehicles) in both the Motorbike and Car classes.

section.para: There is no longer any need for a VehicleType enumeration. By making the type attribute the type designator for the Vehicle class, we are implicitly restricting the set of allowed values for that attribute to the list of names that represent the known descendants of the Vehicle class (including the Vehicle itself). That is, LinkML-aware tools will automatically enforce that the value of type is one of Vehicle, Bicycle, MotorizedVehicle, Motorbike, or Car.

Furthermore, there is no need for any explicit rules restricting the use of some attributes depending on the value of the type attribute. This is automatically handled by the type designation system. LinkML-aware tools will know that, when the type is set to, say, Motorbike, then a power value is allowed, but a windshield_surface value is not.
